report:
## Report

The claim is well-supported by strong evidence and is **not false**—the scientific consensus and data clearly show the adjuvanted recombinant zoster vaccine (RZV, Shingrix) significantly reduces shingles in adults 70 and older.

The pivotal ZOE-70 trial (Cunningham et al., NEJM 2016), a large randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind phase 3 trial enrolling nearly 14,000 adults ≥70 years across 18 countries, found RZV had a vaccine efficacy of approximately 89.8% against herpes zoster in this age group—substantially higher than the older live zoster vaccine (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1603800). This finding was consistent with results from the companion ZOE-50 trial in adults ≥50, which showed even higher efficacy (97.2%) (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1501184).

Long-term follow-up data (ZOSTER-049 extension study) confirm durable protection: efficacy remained high roughly 10 years post-vaccination, and CDC states immunity remains strong for at least 7 years in adults 70+ with healthy immune systems (https://www.cdc.gov/shingles/vaccines/index.html). Real-world observational evidence corroborates trial results—a 2025 target-trial-emulation study using Medicare claims data, published in Annals of Internal Medicine, found RZV highly effective in adults 65+, including immunocompromised individuals, with two doses outperforming one (https://www.med.unc.edu/fammed/2025/10/21/unc-study-confirms-shingles-vaccine-effectiveness-in-older-adults/).

Based on randomized controlled trial data, extended follow-up studies, and real-world effectiveness research, the evidence strongly supports—rather than contradicts—the claim that RZV reduces shingles incidence in adults aged 70 and older. This consensus underlies CDC's routine recommendation of Shingrix for this population.
